analysis.investment_thesis: Wakefit is a loss-making consumer brand with three consecutive years of negative net income (-₹146 Cr, -₹15 Cr, -₹35 Cr), no dividend history, and a P/B of 4.35x — failing every quantitative filter I require. At a market cap of ₹4,905 Cr against a balance sheet producing no real earnings, the investor is paying entirely for speculative growth hopes, not proven earning power.
key_strengths: Revenue growing steadily: ₹797 Cr → ₹1,256 Cr (+57.6% over two years), suggesting real market demand.
EBITDA turned positive in 2024-25 (₹56 Cr, ₹83 Cr), hinting at eventual operating leverage if costs are controlled.
Free cash flow positive in FY24 (₹52 Cr) and FY25 (₹26 Cr) — one genuine bright spot in an otherwise bleak picture.
key_risks: Persistent net losses all three years; EPS is negative, rendering P/E of 118x meaningless — there are no earnings to price.
Debt surging from ₹144 Cr to ₹273 Cr (+89%) while cash collapsed to just ₹7 Cr — liquidity and solvency risk are rising simultaneously.
P/B of 4.35x means the buyer pays far above asset value for a business that is actively destroying equity (₹544 Cr → ₹521 Cr in one year).
red_flags: Zero positive net income in any of the three years on record — fails my minimum 3-5 year earnings requirement outright.
Graham Number is incalculable: negative EPS makes any price a speculative premium with no mathematical floor.
Cash position near zero (₹7 Cr) against ₹273 Cr in debt and ₹30 Cr annual finance costs — thin margin for error.
ROE of -6.72% and ROCE of -1.05%: management is destroying shareholder capital, not compounding it.
Recently incorporated (2016), recently listed — classic IPO where the seller's bankers have priced the offering to benefit the issuer, not the buyer.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By every quantitative test I have applied over decades, Wakefit fails conclusively. The Graham Number requires positive EPS — there is none. P/B at 4.35x is nearly three times my ceiling of 1.5x, meaning the investor pays ₹4.35 for every ₹1 of net assets in a company that is shrinking those assets. Debt/equity of 0.50 sits right at my outer tolerance, but with cash of only ₹7 Cr and finance costs of ₹30 Cr annually, the balance sheet offers no real cushion. There is no dividend, no earnings track record, and no margin of safety — only a story about a growing home-furnishings brand.

The revenue trajectory (₹797 → ₹1,256 Cr) and improving EBITDA (₹-87 Cr → ₹83 Cr) tell an optimistic operational story, but Mr. Market has already priced that story at an EV/EBITDA of 54.88x. I do not pay 55 times EBITDA for a business that has never earned a rupee of net profit. The intelligent investor waits for a price that embeds safety against being wrong; at ₹148.6 per share, this price embeds only the assumption that everything goes right. That is speculation, not investment.
